Summary by release

After the weight figures were released in the Gen4 release (2026-08-13), later commits revised ads brand-safety verdicts, Grok-based policy verdicts, Phoenix training and serving, and visibility-filtering several times.

  • On 2026-08-13, the Gen4 release published the weight figures in the production cron mirror file. (daily)
    • The published file is home-mixer/params/param.rs.
    • Example values are reply 5.0, favorite 0.5, retweet 1.0, share via copy link 20.0, and report −234.
    • Original posts from mutual follows get a reply +15 boost.
  • The 2026-08-14 commit (Gen4+1) added a code comment that corrects a misreading of the weights and a Brazil 2026 election filter. Cold-start Thompson sampling, 14-day stale post gating, and a partial release of the BDSM enforcement note generator came with it. (c65aa17, daily)
    • The code comment explicitly warns “do not read ratio as a raw-count equivalent”.
    • The Brazil 2026 election filter hardcoded 665 accounts and has a following exception.
  • The 2026-08-17 commit (Gen4+2) added ads brand-safety verdict V2 v1 and a cross-validation layer for adult content verdicts. The indexing gate in Phoenix retrieval was removed. (b089ce6, daily)
  • The 2026-08-18 commit (Gen4+3) redesigned the ads safety V2 helper after one day. A Following-only VF hydrator, the SID connection in VMRanker, Phoenix Kafka v3, and the grox reply_spam unification also came with it. (11a71f8, daily)
  • The 2026-08-19 commit (Gen4+4) changed the default Phoenix training optimizer from Adam to Muon and expanded Phoenix to search ranking. It also included Following pipeline hardening, a Grok 4.6 dial, and VF shadow mirroring. (aad7179, daily)
    1. Phoenix training switched from Adam to the Muon optimizer.
      • The default dense-parameter optimizer changed to optax-based Muon (Newton-Schulz orthogonalization).
      • It is a hybrid in which embeddings, norms, and logits still use Adam.
      • The new base learning rate is 7.1e-4; the previous value was 1e-3.
    2. Phoenix expanded to search ranking.
      • A new config xrecsys_search appeared and uses a separate vocab (100M user/item, 30M author).
      • history_seq_len is 1022, and it is set with use_product_surface=True and condition_search_relevance_on_prompt=True.
    3. A RewardOutputs message (values, policyLogits) and a rewardRerankSlotProb field were introduced in the Phoenix proto.
      • These two are scaffolding for reward-based re-ranking.
      • A 5-quantile head for link-open probability (P10/P25/P50/P75/P90) was also added.
    4. A Following-side FollowingViewerMutedKeywordFilter and a QuotedPostTextHydrator were newly introduced, continuing the Following pipeline hardening.
      • The two new pieces of code are 65 lines and 106 lines, respectively.
    5. A Grok 4.6 internal 10% dial was introduced in grox PTOS (_GROK_4_6_INTERNAL_DIAL = 0.1).
      • A new prior_nsfw.py was also introduced. Posts already flagged NSFW by a Manhattan lookup skip reclassification.
    6. dark_traffic_setup.rs (109 new lines) was added to visibility-filtering.
      • Gated by env, only specific ordinal pods mirror requests to the xai-vf-shadow.prod.visibility shadow deployment.
    7. Four features were promoted to train-default ON in the default Phoenix training config _home_direct_packed_base().
      • The four features are enable_stale_post=True, enable_is_author_followed_by_viewer=True, enable_is_author_following_viewer=True, and enable_engagement_counts=True.
      • The three bool features whose values were populated in the 2026-08-14 commit (Gen4+1) became default training inputs starting with this commit.
  • In the 2026-08-20 commit (Gen4+5), a hydrator that attaches AI trend labels to For You candidates was added, and the slate context produced by serving began to be connected to ranking. (d0cef2f, daily)
    1. An AI trend feedback context hydrator was introduced (157 lines).
      • It attaches an "AI trend" label to For You candidates as a second context channel alongside topic feedback.
      • It picks the top-2 trends by candidate frequency and randomly picks one candidate per trend.
      • The landing URL is https://x.com/i/trending/{trend_id}.
      • The target condition is standalone original post, non-topic, non-in-network.
    2. The wiring of served_slate_context began.
      • The actual pipeline started consuming the proto prepared in the 2026-08-19 commit (Gen4+4).
      • PhoenixScorer extracts candidate_slate_context() from the prediction response and sets it.
      • Depending on the UseServedSlateContext gate, RankingScorer uses the slate context produced by serving as is, instead of local computation and cache. There are three fallback paths.
      • This slate context holds pool_rank, fatigue, pre_diversity, three SID layers, and three SID gap layers.
    3. emb_table.rs was refactored (+189/−169).
      • It split load_tensor into a pyo3-free core (load_tensor_into) and a Python wrapper.
      • It replaced the tokio runtime unwrap() with map_err.
      • It added a checkpoint path too short guard.
    4. The Grok 4.6 internal dial rose from 0.1 to 0.3, a 3× increase in one day.
    5. grok_sampler gained a stop_predicate callback and aclosing.
      • Streaming early termination and the llm.sample.early_stop.count counter were added together.
    6. A profile_image field was introduced in the grox User schema.
  • The 2026-08-21 commit (Gen4+6) introduced 20 ads conversion actions and a training-loss branch for delayed feedback. The Muon optimizer was formally included in the export, and Grok 4.5 internal was removed entirely. (28e414f, daily)
    1. 20 ads conversion actions were introduced at proto ActionName 171–190.
      • 6 MACT in-app event types × 2 click/view families = 12. The events are purchase, add_to_cart, level_achieved, tutorial_complete, sign_up, and custom.
      • On top of these come 8 view-through conversions: purchase/add_to_cart/checkout_initiated/sign_up/site_visit/session/landing_page_view/upper_funnel.
    2. split_head_training_by_source branches delayed feedback out of the training loss.
      • When the is_delayed_feedback column is passed through kafka, it arrives as the sample_source batch field.
      • The loss mask then splits so that the engagement head trains only on fresh samples and the conversion head trains only on delayed samples.
      • The fresh/delayed_clicked/delayed_non_clicked metric slices were introduced.
      • mact_in_app_loss_weight, train_view_through_heads, and conversion_keep_mask were exposed as tuning knobs.
      • The new metric group ads_slim consists of 3 positives, 4 negatives, and non-primary conversion click.
      • CLIENT_TWEET_SEARCH_QUERY_REFORMULATED was added to negative feedback.
    3. The Muon optimizer was formally included in the export.
      • TRAINING.md and the README were rewritten to say "flagship ranking config + home_direct_packed_nano trained end-to-end with the production Muon recipe".
      • Embedding rowwise AdaGrad includes three options: accumulator half-life decay, lazy per-row decay, and decoupled weight decay.
    4. The nano config inherited the LR and optimizer settings of the NVIDIA GB300 hardware override that has existed since the Gen4 release.
      • _GB300_OVERRIDES defines bs_per_device=512, ep=64, and attn_impl="cutedsl_ranker_varlen_attn".
      • remat_policy=RematType.SAVE_GB300_RECSYS, unroll_layer_stack=True, and LR 5e-4 are also defined in the same override.
      • home_direct_packed_nano inherits this override.
    5. The interface of the xai-o2 storage crate was released.
      • The BaseO2Client trait of an S3-compatible object storage client and 15 builder methods were exposed.
      • However, build() always returns the error "the xai-o2 backend is not included in this build". The implementation is not public.
    6. SlateContext was added as field #9 of NextActionDistribution (a slate context per action distribution).
    7. The grox reply_spam follower threshold rose from 60k → 80k.
      • Four successive raises were made over 10 days, and this one is a modest 1.33×.
    8. The visibility-filtering dark_traffic target changed from shadow to staging.
      • xai-vf-shadow.prod.visibility was renamed to xai-vf-service.staging.visibility:grpc, and the TLS domain also moved to .staging..
      • ⚠ This change reinterprets the shadow description in the 2026-08-19 commit (Gen4+4).
    9. Grok 4.5 internal was removed completely.
      • The 4.6 dial started in the 2026-08-19 commit (Gen4+4) went 0.1→0.3→100% and finished within two days. It targeted the child safety judge and the deluxe reclassification, not the adult content judge of Gen4+2.
      • _eapi_4_5_internal_breaker, _sample_4_5_internal, and _GROK_4_6_INTERNAL_DIAL were all deleted.
    10. Added 65k-row chunking to retrieval post-embedding.
    11. Added a --hotswap_malloc_trim option to hotswap, and documented a memory leak of ~196MiB per cycle.
  • In the 2026-08-24 commit (Gen4+7), a staging-only harness appeared that compares VF verdicts against a reference VF on every request, and ads brand safety verdicts grew to four levels. Grok 4.5 re-entered as a judge that only allows demotion in three PTOS categories. (d011592, daily)
    1. The VF reference comparison harness was added as a new file, visibility-filtering/reference_compare.rs (812 lines).
      • On every request, this harness calls StratoVfClient, the Strato-based reference VF, in parallel and strictly compares the result with the verdict the service produced.
      • The two count as equal only if action and reason match exactly (is_exact_match).
      • When they differ, it logs a JSON line. The line budget is 12KiB.
      • The metrics are vf_reference_compared/exact_match/differed/error/skipped/enabled.
      • It is gated by the environment variables VF_DUAL_CALL_HARNESS_ENABLED and APP_ENV. With APP_ENV=prod it panics at boot, which enforces staging-only use.
      • This is a new canary that compares actual verdicts, separate from dark_traffic (which only mirrors traffic).
    2. The brand safety verdict expanded to four levels.
      • BrandSafetyVerdict::HighRisk = 4 was introduced.
      • Five labels that were in medium were promoted to HighRisk: NSFW_HIGH_PRECISION, NSFW_HIGH_RECALL, GORE_AND_VIOLENCE_HIGH_PRECISION, PDNA, EGREGIOUS_NSFW.
      • The new SOFT_NSFW is also HighRisk.
      • V2 moved symmetrically.
      • The ads utility has_avoid() treats both Medium and High as avoid.
      • The NSFW ancestor promotion in ads_brand_safety_vf_hydrator.rs changed from Medium to High.
      • scored_posts_server.rs introduced proto HM enum mappings for five V2 labels and exposes them downstream. The labels are GROK_SFA_V2, GROK_NSFA_LIMITED_V2, GROK_NSFA_V2, GROK_NSFA_EXPANDED_V2, and PTOS_REVIEWED.
    3. The PTOS policy verdict cross-validator expanded to three categories.
      • After Grok 4.5 internal was removed in the 2026-08-21 commit (Gen4+6), the new judge class uses EAPI_GROK_4_5_X_ALGO, which the adult content judge has used since Gen4+2. It is judge-only, not primary.
      • The new class SafetyPtosPolicyCrossValidator rechecks the primary verdict with 4.5 in three categories, ChildSafety, ViolentMedia, and IllegalAndRegulatedBehaviors, and allows only demotion.
      • When there is a disagreement, the verdict changes to NoViolation or a lighter policy.
      • It exists alongside the adult content judge (SafetyPtosAdultContentCrossValidationJudge) from the 2026-08-17 commit (Gen4+2).
      • USE_REASONING_CATEGORIES = {ViolentSpeech, SuicideOrSelfHarm} and USE_THREAD_RENDERER_CATEGORIES were introduced.
      • Only in these two categories does it lift the thinking constraint and feed the parent thread to the renderer (harm cannot be judged without context).
    4. The Phoenix checkpoint loader was hardened for multi-node production.
      • The following arguments were introduced in xai_checkpointing/load.py:
        • domains: per-tensor ts.IndexDomain slices
        • tag: checkpoint subdirectory, default "orbax-ckpt"
        • concurrent_gb: byte throttle for concurrent decoding
      • The XAI_RESTORE_NODE_SERIALIZE environment variable (on by default) serializes restore on each node with fcntl.flock(). The path is /dev/shm/xai_restore_node_lock.

Gen4+4 (2026-08-19) — visibility-filtering shadow deployment (xai-vf-shadow) wiring

The 2026-08-19 commit (Gen4+4) attached request mirroring (dark traffic) to the VF service, so production requests can be copied to a shadow deployment verified. This created a base for shadow-verifying VF policy changes with production traffic, but which rule experiments run on top of it is not public. This commit was covered in the daily.

Request mirroring (dark traffic) infrastructure was attached to the VF service itself verified — visibility-filtering/dark_traffic_setup.rs (109 lines, new). This layer is connected in visibility-filtering/main.rs verified.

Mirroring is gated by three environment variables:

  • DARK_TRAFFIC_ENABLED (bool, default false) is the master switch.
  • ORDINAL_NUMBER is the index of this pod (StatefulSet ordinal, etc.).
  • DARK_TRAFFIC_MAX_ORDINAL (default 1) is the threshold that turns dark traffic on only when ord < max. In other words, by default only pod ordinal 0 mirrors, and max is raised only in specific deployments so that several pods mirror.

The mirroring target is xai-vf-shadow.prod.visibility:grpc, hardcoded through StaticShadowDiscovery. The per-datacenter domain override is visibility.visibility-filtering-service.prod.{DATACENTER}.s2s.twttr.net (default atla). mTLS is required (TlsMode::mtls_from_env).

⚠ In Gen4+6 (2026-08-21, 28e414f), the name of this target changed to xai-vf-service.staging.visibility:grpc. The TLS domain also moved to visibility.visibility-filtering-service.staging.{dc}.s2s.twttr.net, and StaticShadowDiscovery became StaticStagingDiscovery. In other words, dark_traffic was redefined within three days from "mirroring a production shadow workload" to "mirroring the staging environment". There are two interpretations.

  • One is that this is an infrastructure cleanup: staging is used as the shadow instead of maintaining a separate shadow workload.
  • The other is that a production-traffic shadow was judged to have value for verifying staging deployments.

Either way, VF experiments now run on the staging resource budget rather than on production shadow resources.

⚠ In Gen4+16 (2026-09-04, 902a06f), the mirroring targets expanded to two app_env values, staging and devel verified — visibility-filtering/dark_traffic_setup.rs.

  • The function name changed from parse_staging_listener to parse_mirror_listener, and it iterates over the two app_env values (STAGING_APP_ENV = "staging" and DEVEL_APP_ENV = "devel").
  • MirrorChannelFactory assigns a channel factory by choosing the devel TLS domain if the listener xds_dest contains .devel., and the staging TLS domain otherwise.
    • The devel TLS domain is visibility.xai-vf-service.devel.{dc}.s2s.twttr.net.
  • An example that passes is xai-vf-service-pr-123.devel.visibility:grpc. It suggests a practice of preview deployments based on GitHub PR numbers inferred.
  • The rejection cases are strict. Similar names such as development, staging-devel, and grpc-extra are explicitly rejected.

Which requests to mirror is decided by the rules in /config/dark-traffic/dark_traffic.yaml. ReloadableDarkTrafficConfigBuilder re-reads this dynamic config whenever the file changes.

Why it matters: This created a base for shadow-verifying VF service policy changes with production traffic. Examples of policy changes are the removal of the favoriteCount>=1 gate in Gen4+3, dark_traffic itself in Gen4+4, and future rule tuning. VF is fail-closed (the fail-closed item in the safety section), so rule changes carry high risk, and a shadow deployment is naturally required infrastructure for this pipeline. Which rule experiments actually run on top of it is not public. The actual dark_traffic.yaml is not in the repo.

Gen4+7 (2026-08-24) — Wiring the VF reference comparison harness (reference_compare.rs)

The 2026-08-24 commit (Gen4+7) added a harness in which staging VF also calls a Strato-backed reference VF on each request, strictly compares the two verdicts, and logs only the differences verified. Viewed together with the dark traffic introduced in Gen4+4 and redirected to staging in Gen4+6, this harness is infrastructure that measures, at production traffic scale, how closely the VF rewrite matches the original so far. This commit was covered in the daily.

While dark_traffic only mirrored traffic, this release added a canary that compares actual verdicts verified — visibility-filtering/reference_compare.rs (812 lines, new). The files changed alongside are visibility-filtering/filter_tweets.rs, visibility-filtering/server_deps.rs, and visibility-filtering/config.rs.

The harness does not change the response; a separate task compares against the verdict of the reference VF.

  • FilterTweetsEndpoint holds an Option<Arc<ReferenceCompareHarness>>. On each request it calls harness.begin_compare(viewer_id, country_code, safety_level, tweet_ids), spawns a separate tokio task, and sends a parallel request to the Strato-backed reference VF.
    • The reference VF is wrapped by StratoVfClient and is likely the Gen1 and Gen2 Scala VF stack inferred. The Gen3 public code is Rust/Python, so it has no Scala VF.
    • The main path sends its own verdict to the harness task through a oneshot::channel, but the response is not affected (read-only).
  • Once the harness task receives both results, it strictly compares the verdict for each tweet_id with compare_batch(). The criterion is is_exact_match(): the service action and reference action labels must be exactly equal, and FilteredReason must also match completely.
  • Differing verdicts are collected as Diff { tweet_id, service, reference }. After grouping them into tweet_id lists by identical (service, reference) string pairs, it emits JSON lines chunked to a 12KiB line budget to stdout with println!(), into the log stream.
    • The format of each line is {h: "vf_reference_compare", v: 1, batch, chunk, build, dc, level, viewer, diffs: [...]}.
  • There are six metrics. Every metric carries a build_sha tag, so regressions of a specific build can be tracked.
    • vf_reference_compared (comparisons completed), _exact_match (matches), _differed (mismatches)
    • _error (kind=timeout|reference_item|missing_result), _skipped (reason=level_unmapped|logged_out_viewer), _enabled (once at harness boot)

The harness restricts when it is enabled, where it runs, what it compares, and how long it waits.

  • The master switch is the VF_DUAL_CALL_HARNESS_ENABLED environment variable (bool).
  • It also checks APP_ENV. should_build_harness(flag, app_env) returns Err("VF_DUAL_CALL_HARNESS_ENABLED is set but APP_ENV=prod; the reference comparator is staging-only") for (true, Some("prod")). server_deps.rs escalates this Err into a panic!(), so boot fails. In other words, the harness is enforced as staging-only at the code level.
  • Only SafetyLevel::TimelineHome and TimelineHomeRecommendations are compared. FilterAll, which is not in the reference VF code either, is skipped. Logged-out viewers are also skipped.
  • The reference call timeout is 1.5 seconds. If it is exceeded, only an ERROR "timeout" metric is recorded and the task ends quietly.

How this harness differs from dark_traffic and shadow becomes clear when the three commits are placed side by side:

  • Gen4+4 (aad7179, 08-19): dark_traffic_setup.rs copies the production traffic requests themselves to xai-vf-shadow.prod.visibility. It only consumes traffic resources and does no verdict comparison. The dark side's response is not visible anyway.
  • Gen4+6 (28e414f, 08-21): The name of the dark_traffic target changed from shadow prod to staging. In other words, production traffic verifies the staging deployment as a shadow.
  • Gen4+7 (d011592, 08-24): reference_compare.rs runs in the staging deployment (the currently running process is staging). On each request it calls the reference VF (the Strato-backed earlier generation) in parallel, strictly compares the verdicts, and logs only the diffs. In other words, when traffic sent by the dark_traffic stack arrives at this staging service, the service computes its own verdict and at the same time checks it against the Strato reference.

Combining the two layers gives this chain: production traffic → dark_traffic → staging VF → comparison against the Strato reference in reference_compare → diff log. In other words, what this release really delivers is infrastructure that measures, at production traffic scale, how closely the VF rewrite matches the original so far. The VF rewrite was one of Gen4's headline sub-repos, and VF is item #1 on the canon caveat list (fail-closed, high rule-change risk). That verification channel is now complete.

Undisclosed:

  • Exactly which VF stack StratoVfClient wraps (whether a remnant of the Gen1 and Gen2 Scala VF or a separate stack)
  • By what rules dark_traffic.yaml selects requests
  • Whether diffs go out only as logs or a separate dashboard is attached
  • The production promotion threshold (for example, "promote if the diff rate is below X%")

Phoenix checkpoint stack save/restore double hardening — Gen4+7 (restore, 2026-08-24) + Gen4+9 (save, streamed restore, warm-start staging, 2026-08-26)

The 2026-08-24 commit (Gen4+7) capped the bytes read concurrently when restoring a checkpoint and serialized restores per node verified. We read it as a change to prevent the host OOMs that occurred when several workers restored a model enlarged since the Muon generation at the same time inferred. The 2026-08-26 commit (Gen4+9) added a byte budget and per-node serialization to the save side, plus streamed restore that feeds batches and warm-start staging verified. The restore side was covered in the Gen4+7 daily, the save side in the Gen4+9 daily.

Gen4+7 refactored the checkpoint loader to cap host memory use of concurrent restores verified — phoenix/python/training/xai-checkpointing/xai_checkpointing/load.py (+178/−36). The log string in the code states the purpose of this throttle as bound host transient (line 212 of the same file). The account that models grew after the Muon generation and concurrent restores by multiple workers caused host OOMs is an interpretation not found in the code inferred.

Three new arguments were added to load_checkpoint.

  • domains: dict[str, Any] | None: specifies a ts.IndexDomain slice for each tensor. It is used to load only specific tensors partially, or to state the slice explicitly when the local shape differs from the checkpoint shape.
    • It supports two forms: a JSON spec (ts.IndexDomain(json=domain)) and an indexing expression (ts.IndexDomain(shape=host_state[name].shape)[domain]).
  • tag: str | None = None: the checkpoint subdirectory name, with a default of "orbax-ckpt". The actual path is built as path / tag.
    • That is, the practice of keeping several checkpoint tags (for example "orbax-ckpt", "post-warmup", "muon-recipe-v3") under one base path is reflected in the code.
  • concurrent_gb: float | None: the cap on tensor bytes decoded concurrently. It is converted with int(concurrent_gb * 10**9), and reads are then cut into batches (if cur_bytes + nbytes > concurrent_bytes: flush batch). If None, all reads are issued in parallel without throttling.
    • The log states ACTIVE or no throttle, and it warns when an individual tensor is larger than the throttle budget.

Restore is serialized at the node level verified.

  • It is toggled with the environment variable XAI_RESTORE_NODE_SERIALIZE. The default is "1", and "0"|""|"false" turns it off.
  • The lock file path is set by XAI_RESTORE_NODE_LOCK_FILE. The default is /dev/shm/xai_restore_node_lock, or /tmp/xai_restore_node_lock if /dev/shm does not exist.
  • The _NodeBatchLock class takes an exclusive lock with fcntl.flock(fd, LOCK_EX). It prevents multiple JAX workers on the same node from restoring at the same time. It forces a node to process only one batch at a time, and it logs if it waits one second or more.
  • Between batches, _release_batch_memory() returns glibc allocator slack with gc.collect() and ctypes.CDLL("libc.so.6").malloc_trim(0).

Why it matters: In Gen4+6, TRAINING.md was rewritten as "the flagship ranking config + home_direct_packed_nano train end-to-end with the production Muon recipe" and nano inherited the GB300 override; we infer that the OOM issue in the restore path was found during follow-up batch verification in that generation inferred. Before Gen4, models were small and this infrastructure was not needed. However, at Muon and GB300 scale, multi-worker restore exceeds node memory, so spreading restores over time with the node lock and limiting batch size with concurrent_gb became essential. It is a signal that Gen4's training stack has matured.

Undisclosed:

  • Which tensors are loaded as partial slices (domains), such as which optimizer state for Muon, or embedding table chunking
  • The production tuning value of concurrent_gb
  • How much the node lock lengthens restore time

Gen4+9 (2026-08-26, 45b48ba) unified valid_step gating in trainer_recsys verified — phoenix/xrex/train/trainer_recsys.py (+29/−19).

The param update order changed in two places: the dense sync path and the async_no_deferred path. Previously it proceeded in this order:

  1. Check the dense grad-norm to get valid_step.
  2. Gate the dense params update with valid_step.
  3. After segment_sum, check the emb grad-norm to get emb_valid_step.
  4. Gate only the emb table update with emb_valid_step.
  5. Compute valid_step & emb_valid_step in the metric.

That is, if dense passes and only emb fails, an asymmetric state lasting a few steps could arise in which dense params are updated to new values and only emb is rolled back.

In the changed order, the emb check comes before the dense update.

  1. Check the dense grad-norm to get valid_step.
  2. First, after segment_sum, check the emb grad-norm to get emb_valid_step.
  3. Compute keep_step = valid_step & emb_valid_step.
  4. Gate the dense params update with keep_step.
  5. Gate the emb update with sparse_update(..., valid_step=keep_step) as well.
  6. Unify the metric on keep_step too.

The async_no_deferred path was also aligned to AsyncEmbGradientUpdate.pending=keep_step (previously jnp.asarray(True)). Whether the async emb gradient is actually applied at the next step is decided by this step's gate result. Also, assert self.grad_norm_keep_threshold is None in _create_async_emb_executables was removed. Previously it assumed that the async deferred path was incompatible with grad-norm gating; now async also actually uses that threshold.

Why it matters: In the Muon and GB300 generation, dense and embedding grads were probably observed spiking at different scales inferred. Lock-step gating blocks the residual effects of that divergence at the source, and because dense and the embedding table move only in lock-step, reproducible training consistency is secured. The metrics also keep three separate observation fields: valid_step is dense only, emb_valid_step is emb only, and deferred_emb_grad_norm/valid_step is for the deferred family. These fields make it possible to diagnose at which layer the gate triggered.

Gen4+9 (2026-08-26, 45b48ba) hardened the save side symmetrically to the restore side, and added streamed restore and warm-start staging verified — phoenix/xrex/utils/checkpointing.py (+215/−6). The files changed alongside are phoenix/python/training/xai-checkpointing/xai_checkpointing/load.py (+311/−88) and phoenix/xrex/train/trainer.py (+39/−8).

  • Save-side ThrottledD2HArrayHandler: the D2H budget can now be set with the save_checkpoint(..., save_concurrent_gb=<N>) argument.
    • It overrides Orbax ArrayHandler.serialize and groups tensors into batches by addressable_nbytes. For each batch it calls super().serialize(), waits for future.result(), and then moves on to the next batch.
    • Previously, Orbax's write-limiter only capped the save bottleneck at a 96GB default, while the D2H (device-to-host copy) itself staged everything, and host OOM occurred at this stage.
    • If compressed, it registers ThrottledD2HArrayHandler; otherwise it registers ThrottledNoCompressionArrayHandler (multiple inheritance with NoCompressionArrayHandler).
  • Save node-serialize: fully symmetric to the node-serialize pattern of the Gen4+7 restore.
    • It takes a flock exclusive lock with the XAI_SAVE_NODE_SERIALIZE=1 env and XAI_SAVE_NODE_LOCK_FILE (default /dev/shm/xai_save_node_lock).
    • It calls _release_batch_memory() between batches (gc.collect() and malloc_trim(0)).
  • load_checkpoint_streamed: a new function. The earlier load_checkpoint first built host_state (a pinned-host copy of all tensors). The streamed version leaves device_state as is and, for each batch, goes through pinned-host stage of only that batch's tensors → file read → move to device with device_put → free the batch's host memory.
    • The auto-window is min(max(max_leaf, total/16), 32GB) (window_gb=None by default), and window_gb can also be set explicitly.
    • It sorts with plan.sort(key=lambda item: item[3], reverse=True) so that large tensors are processed first.
    • When the old/new array pairs of a completed batch are passed to the on_replaced callback, the caller updates and releases the references.
    • copy_aliased_arrays separates aliased references beforehand.
  • Trainer.warm_start_staging_spec hook: in a warm start that restores only params from the checkpoint and re-initializes opt_state, it no longer makes an opt_state copy in pinned-host either.
    • Previously, when it did device_put with the staging sharding for restore, the entire state went up to pinned-host. Now it cuts out the opt_state fields in advance with warm_purge(self.state), stages to pinned-host, and then device_puts only the loaded part back to device. The original opt_state field is kept.
    • RecsysTrainer supports a keep_emb_opt_state=True option through an override (keeps only emb_table_state).
    • The save and restore stack atomically supports the standard flow in which flagship Muon training starts with pretrained params and a fresh optimizer.
  • admission.reset_estimates and request_metrics.reset_admission_estimates: reset the service_time and pipeline_time EWMAs of the Phoenix serving admission controller to zero. Prometheus gauges are aligned as well, and there are two regression tests. This is likely for resetting the EWMA immediately after a sudden change in traffic profile or a hot-swap inferred.
  • copy_port_client logging cleanup: the completion logs of the dense weights load and the emb_table load now include total bytes, elapsed time, and GB/s (with a divide-by-zero guard). The start log was removed, and the end log now serves as the summary.

Why it matters: After Gen4+6 formally included flagship Muon training in the export, there was probably an observation that when multiple workers save, checkpoint save causes host OOM in the D2H stage outside wait_until_finished inferred. The logic is symmetric to the restore side of Gen4+7. The warm start scenario points toward standardizing the flow in which the flagship starts with pretrained params and a fresh optimizer, so both the save stack and the restore stack were optimized for this usage pattern. The Gen4+7 → +9 flow is understood as "reorganizing the whole Muon+GB300 checkpoint round trip into a batched pipeline with an RSS cap".

Undisclosed:

  • The production tuning value of save_concurrent_gb
  • When load_checkpoint_streamed replaces the default load_checkpoint
  • The first config in which warm_start_staging is active
  • The actual call trigger of admission reset_estimates (whether hot-swap completion or traffic shift detection)
  • The target GB/s for copy_port

Gen4+8 (2026-08-25) — AES generic_actions passthrough wiring

Since the 2026-08-25 commit (Gen4+8), AES (abuse-enforcement-service) can pass through not only the static rules written in YAML but also actions requested directly by a scorer, through two layers of allowlists. Attaching a new scorer now needs a shorter YAML deployment cycle, but the actual allowlist values that decide which score maps to which action are outside the public source. This commit was covered in the daily.

In Gen4+8, abuse-enforcement-service/service-lib/src/generic_actions.rs (663 lines, new) was added. Previously, AES executed only rules statically encoded in enforcement_user.yaml / enforcement_post.yaml. For example, it suspends if "llm_slop_user" in score.labels && "SpamHighRecall" in user.labels. Now, when a scorer sends its own score.requested_actions list, AES can pass it through.

Requests are verified in two layers.

  • Hardcoded kind allowlist: contains 5 user kinds (suspend, label, bounce_captcha, bounce_arkose, spam_liveness_check) and 2 post kinds (post_label, suspend_author). The limit is 16 per message.
  • GrowthBook dynamic allowlist: verifies along three axes: kinds, suspend_policies, and labels.

Rejected requests are not discarded; they are recorded in the outcome.info["requested_actions_skipped"] JSON and the GENERIC_ACTION_TOTAL{outcome=skipped, reason} metric, which keeps observability explicit. Scorer teams can immediately see why their request was rejected. The first client was the panda_reports_embedding_v10_rough_spam label of the embedding-based spam detector v10, which appeared as a temporary PlatformManipulation suspend.

Why it matters: Attaching a new scorer now needs a shorter AES YAML deployment cycle, and A/B gating is also possible from the GrowthBook console. However, the mapping itself of "which score maps to which action" (the actual allowlist values in GrowthBook) is still outside the public source.

Gen4+9 (2026-08-26) — TesHydrator media fallback cache removed entirely + dark_traffic canary opt-out

The 2026-08-26 commit (Gen4+9) deleted the fallback cache that could return media features from an earlier lookup when VF failed a TES lookup, and removed canary workloads from dark traffic mirroring verified. The deleted cache was a safety net for the stabilization period after the early VF rewrite inferred. This commit was covered in the daily.

Deleted the media fallback cache verified — visibility-filtering/hydration/tes_hydrator.rs (+4/−292). The following three files changed with it:

  • visibility-filtering/config.rs (0+/20−)
  • visibility-filtering/hydration/mod.rs (+3/−2)
  • visibility-filtering/server_deps.rs (0+/9−)

Previously, TesHydrator (Tweet Entity Service, X's internal tweet metadata lookup service) held a fallback cache based on a 1M-entry LRU. When a TES call failed and no media entity came back, behavior depended on the mode.

  • With FallbackCacheMode::ServeStale, it returned stale but valid media features from a previously successful lookup.
  • With Shadow, it filled the cache but did not use it for serving.
  • With Disabled, it failed without a fallback.

This cache was removed in full this time, and the related code was deleted with it:

  • The CACHE_CAPACITY = 1_000_000 constant and the FallbackCache::new("media", ...) instance field
  • The resolve_hydration_batch call
  • Related regression tests (media_stale_recovery_respects_cache_mode, no_media_tweets_cache_default_entries_that_serve_stale)
  • The mock client (MediaFailingAfterFirstClient)
  • Two environment variables (VF_MEDIA_FALLBACK_CACHE_SERVE_STALE_ENABLED, VF_MEDIA_FALLBACK_CACHE_POPULATE_ENABLED)
  • Config helpers (media_fallback_cache_serve_stale_enabled(), media_fallback_cache_populate_enabled())

The media_fallback_cache_mode: FallbackCacheMode parameter disappeared from the signature of HydrationPipeline::new. The TesHydrator struct now has only one field left: pub tes_client: Arc<dyn TESClient + Send + Sync>.

Why it matters: This fallback cache was a safety net for the stabilization period after the early VF rewrite (the Gen4 headline) inferred. If a failure occurred during the TES infrastructure rewrite, candidates would be caught by fail-close filtering without media features, and this cache mitigated that destructive result. Removing it now means three things:

  • The VF rewrite can now be audited for consistency with the Gen4+7 reference_compare harness.
  • The failure rate of the TES media path has dropped, so the marginal utility of the fallback cache has shrunk.
  • It follows the same "remove the safety net once stabilized" pattern as Gen4+8's major simplification of VMRanker.

However, the fallback caches of other hydrators (such as the gizmoduck author metadata lookup) remain unchanged. The fallback_cache_mode env also still exists.

dark_traffic gained a canary opt-out verified — visibility-filtering/dark_traffic_setup.rs (+40/−17).

  • should_enable(ordinal, max_ordinal) was renamed to should_mirror(workload, ordinal, max_ordinal) and expanded. The new rules are three:
    • If workload=None (env WORKLOAD_NAME unset), it does not mirror, failing closed.
    • If workload.ends_with("-canary"), it does not mirror. Canary workloads are never mirrored to dark_traffic.
    • Otherwise, it decides by ordinal < max_ordinal as before.
  • There are two new tests, canary_never_mirrors (checks the PROD and CANARY constants) and missing_workload_name_fails_closed. The log message was also generalized from "disabled (ordinal >= max)" to "disabled (not a mirror host)".
  • Why it matters: dark_traffic was introduced in Gen4+4 and redefined from shadow to staging in Gen4+6. Now dark_traffic prevents the incident in which a canary workload accidentally enters mirroring and canary issues contaminate shadow verdicts. Because production and canary workloads follow a convention of using the same name prefix inferred, suffix matching suffices.

Gen4+10 (2026-08-28) — sampled async warmer wiring for safety-label twemcache misses

The 2026-08-28 commit (Gen4+10) added a warmer that samples keys missed in the cache while VF looks up safety labels, then rereads them asynchronously to fill the cache verified. Rule verdicts are unchanged; the warmer is a low-level infrastructure optimization that raises the cache hit rate of label lookups. This commit was covered in the daily.

A new file warmer.rs (203 lines) was added under visibility-filtering/safety_label_source/ and attached to the endpoint with RemoteSource::with_warmer(...) verified — visibility-filtering/safety_label_source/warmer.rs (203 lines, new). The following five files changed with it:

  • visibility-filtering/safety_label_source/lookup.rs (+84)
  • visibility-filtering/safety_label_source/metrics.rs (+32)
  • visibility-filtering/config.rs (+85)
  • visibility-filtering/safety_label_source/mod.rs (+1)
  • visibility-filtering/server_deps.rs (+54/−6)

The target is the Strato column visibility/baseTweetSafetyLabelMap. twemcache sits in front of this column as a look-aside cache, and on a miss it falls back to Manhattan. This release adds a warmer channel that re-fetches those misses asynchronously and fills them into twemcache.

The warmer works in four steps:

  1. In RemoteSource::get(ids), twemcache results split into four kinds. Of these, only Miss is collected into a separate vector warm_ids.
    • Hit
    • NotFound: definitively nonexistent
    • Miss: the cache does not know this key
    • FallThrough(reason): cache error, timeout, etc.
    • NotFound, a definitive nonexistence, and FallThrough, which has a fallback reason, are not warming targets. The principle is that warming aims to resolve a state where the cache is not filled, not to respond to misses for other reasons.
  2. Before the Manhattan fallback request goes out, it calls warmer.warm(warm_ids) (fire-and-forget). This does not affect request response latency.
  3. SampledWarmer samples with probability using the VF_CACHE_WARM_SAMPLE_PCT environment variable (0–100, panic on out-of-range). Only the IDs that pass are try_send-ed to a tokio bounded mpsc (capacity 1024).
  4. A background drain task takes vectors from the queue. During a 500ms linger it merges vectors that arrive later and batches up to 50 IDs. It makes a batch_call to Strato with StratoWarmFetcher::fetch(chunk) (WARM_COLUMN_PATH = "visibility/baseTweetSafetyLabelMap").
    • Strato's batch fetch writes the result back to twemcache. We infer that a separate read-through cache layer exists inferred.

Even when the channel is full, the request path is not blocked. If try_send fails (channel full), it only increments the WarmKeyResult::DroppedChannelFull counter and continues request handling. It was designed so that even if the warmer channel saturates, no backpressure is ever applied to the request path. The regression test full_warm_channel_does_not_affect_fallback_result asserts this explicitly.

The observability counter record_cache_warm_keys(result, count) counts 6 outcomes.

  • EligibleMiss: total amount that became warmer targets because of a miss (before sampling)
  • SampledOut: number dropped by sampling
  • Enqueued: number successfully put into the queue
  • DroppedChannelFull: number discarded because the queue was saturated
  • FetchIssued: number actually sent out as Strato calls
  • FetchFailed: number for which the Strato call returned an error

With these 6 outcomes, the pass rate of each warmer stage and its bottleneck can be observed. For example, a high FetchFailed / FetchIssued indicates a Strato infrastructure issue, and a persistent DroppedChannelFull means the channel capacity (1024) is insufficient.

Three side cleanups were also made in the same config.rs. Three new envs appeared: VF_GIZMODUCK_CLIENT_ID, VF_TWEMCACHE_CLIENT_NAME, and APP_ENV. When no value is set, gizmoduck_client_id() assembles the name automatically from the visibility-filtering-service.{APP_ENV|prod} template. That is, the client name for the gizmoduck author metadata lookup splits automatically by deployment environment (staging/prod). We infer that the purpose is to separate the staging gizmoduck quota and rate limit from production when VF runs on staging via dark_traffic (see Gen4+4, +6, +7) inferred.

Why it matters:

  • A twemcache miss has two cases. One is a fresh state where the tweet has not yet received any labeling (neither cache entry nor label exists). The other is TTL expiry or eviction. This warmer addresses especially the second case, that is, the waste of querying Manhattan on every request because the cache missed although Manhattan has the label.
  • Because a sample-pct gate is attached, the warmer itself does not cause a Strato flood even when traffic spikes. A dial-up rollout is possible, starting with VF_CACHE_WARM_SAMPLE_PCT low (for example, 5–10) and raising it gradually. This is a practice similar to Gen4's other dial-up pattern (Grok 4.6 10%→30%→100%).
  • This does not mean a new "request-path layer" of VF has opened. Rule verdicts (3-tier / 54 rules) are unchanged, and this change is a low-level infrastructure optimization that raises the cache hit rate of label lookups. However, VF performs label lookups for tens to hundreds of candidate tweets on every request, so the cache hit rate directly affects P99 latency.

Undisclosed:

  • The initial production value of VF_CACHE_WARM_SAMPLE_PCT
  • How the twemcache miss rate changes before and after the warmer was introduced
  • How the warmer delay (linger 500ms) interacts with the twemcache stale window

Gen4+10 (2026-08-28, 24c6094) — MultiRiskAdsBlender introduced (BSR-high ads tier + medium-risk fallback slot)

The 2026-08-28 commit (Gen4+10) added a fourth ads blender that, only for ads whose advertiser allows impressions in medium-risk context, opens slots between medium-risk posts before safe slots verified. This blender is not the default yet; it is enabled only when selected by a param. This commit was covered in the daily.

A fourth variant, multi_risk, was added to the set of three ads blenders (safe_gap, partition_organic, time_gap) verified — home-mixer/ads/multi_risk_blender.rs (332 lines, new). The other changed files are the test home-mixer/ads/tests/multi_risk_blender_tests.rs (215 lines, new) and home-mixer/selectors/blender_selector.rs (+8/−4).

  • This blender is selected when the AdsBlenderType param receives the string "multi_risk".
  • The same commit added the "partition_organic_low_risk" alias to PartitionOrganicAdsBlender, bringing the options to 5 in total.
    • safe_gap / partition_organic / partition_organic_low_risk / time_gap / multi_risk

The slot policy is set by an adjacency matrix of ad tier and post tier. It combines two axes, BrandSafetyVerdict::HighRisk (introduced in Gen4+7, 2026-08-24; see the section above) and the ad-side AdAdjacencyControl.brand_safety_risk = BsrNormal | BsrHigh, to decide the slot policy.

Ad tier Next to Safe Next to MediumRisk Next to HighRisk
BsrNormal (default) Placed Not placed Not placed
BsrHigh (advertiser opt-in) Placed Placed Not placed

In other words, the earlier blenders (safe_gap, partition_organic) enforced a symmetric policy of "all ads → Safe slots only". By contrast, multi_risk opens medium-medium slots when the advertiser voluntarily allows exposure in medium-risk context (BsrHigh). A HighRisk post cannot be adjacent to any ad.

The safe slot budget is the smallest of three caps.

  • spacing_cap = (n − 1) / requested_spacing (default 3): the cap through which feed length enforces ad spacing.
  • safe_count / 2: each ad slot sits between 2 posts, above and below, so half is the cap.

Which cap was the binding constraint is stated explicitly by the tag MultiRisk.serving_limitation{factor=ads_supply|spacing|safe_posts}. With this tag, the cause of ads not being shown can be sliced in real time into insufficient ad supply, insufficient spacing, and insufficient safe posts.

BsrHigh ads use the spots between medium-risk posts first. If a medium-risk post pair remains, a BsrHigh ad is placed above and below that pair first, and if it fails the overlap check while safe slot budget remains, it moves to a safe slot verified — multi_risk_blender.rs:96-130. However, it must still pass the handle overlap check (handle_drop) and the keyword overlap check (keyword_drop). It is dropped if the advertiser handle is mentioned in a neighboring post or the ad keyword overlaps the neighboring post text. In other words, BsrHigh's medium-risk placement only resolves "the advertiser's contract that placing next to a medium-risk post is acceptable", and the prevention of adjacency self-interference (same advertiser mention, same topic) stays as it was.

Slot outcomes are counted in finer detail with the MultiRisk.slot_outcome{outcome=filled|unfilled_bsr_low|unfilled_handle|unfilled_keyword|unfilled_no_ads} counter.

  • filled: an ad was successfully placed in the slot
  • unfilled_bsr_low: the candidate ad was dropped by the BSR-low signal, and the slot ended up empty
  • unfilled_handle, unfilled_keyword: dropped in the self-interference checks above
  • unfilled_no_ads: ad supply itself was exhausted

SlotRejections::stuck_outcome() picks the most frequent of the three rejection reasons as the slot's representative cause. That is, an A/B dashboard can show "the safety filter hit most often when a slot was empty".

Enforcement results are aggregated in the MultiRisk.enforcement{action=drop|ok|handle_drop|keyword_drop} counter.

  • drop/ok: BSR-low ad decision (dropped or placed)
  • handle_drop/keyword_drop: dropped in the self-interference checks

Why it matters:

  • The five-day flow of Gen4+7 (2026-08-24) HighRisk tier introduced → Gen4+9 ad pixel·conv_asset_ids → Gen4+10 tier×tier matrix blender introduced is now complete. Since HighRisk was split out as a tier and the ad pixel conversion head was attached, a blender option that lets advertisers opt in on the tier axis for their own exposure has now arrived.
  • Crucially, MultiRiskAdsBlender is not yet the default. It is enabled only when the AdsBlenderType param string is "multi_risk". That is, it sits behind an experiment gate, so the actual exposure ratio is not public. The next checkpoint to watch is when the default of AdsBlenderType is promoted to multi_risk.
  • For advertisers, it signals that the incentive structure of BSR-high opt-in is now explicit in the code. Accepting medium-risk context earns medium-risk slots and increases total impressions. Previously, no such slot existed in the code.

Undisclosed:

  • The experiment rollout ratio of AdsBlenderType
  • The actual share of the BsrHigh ad segment (advertiser opt-in adoption rate)
  • How much uplift medium-medium placement produces in revenue and brand safety metrics
  • Deployment practice for the other AdAdjacencyControl fields (handles, keywords)

Gen4+10 (2026-08-28, 24c6094) — trainer actually consumes streamed restore + gRPC trailer preservation bugfix + copy_port shard-schedule shuffle

Depending on a config flag, the Phoenix trainer now actually calls streamed restore, which loads a checkpoint while moving tensors to the device one at a time verified. This commit also fixed a bug where the gRPC status trailer disappeared when compressing serving responses, and shuffled the order in which each pod receives tensor shards so that requests do not pile onto the peer holding the first shard verified — daily covering this commit.

Three-way hardening came out of one commit. The scaffolding that Gen4+9 laid (save symmetry, the load_checkpoint_streamed API, copy_port GB/s logging) matured in three ways in this commit.

  • Connected the consumer on the trainer side.
  • Restored the integrity of the serving response trailer.
  • Spread the peer load of copy_port evenly.

1. The trainer reads the restore_streamed flag and actually uses streamed restore verified — phoenix/xrex/train/trainer.py (+102/−31), phoenix/xrex/configs/xrecsys.py (+1), phoenix/python/training/xai-checkpointing/xai_checkpointing/load.py (+85/−30):

maybe_load_checkpoint now reads the checkpoint_config.restore_streamed flag and actually calls load_checkpoint_streamed. The streamed path is enabled under three conditions, and all must be true.

  • restore_streamed=True
  • ctx.checkpoint.format == "orbax"
  • save_method != "tensorstore"

If any one does not hold, it logs and falls back to the existing load_checkpoint (full pinned-host stage). The use_streamed_restore=True path itself calls checkpointing_load.copy_aliased_arrays(self.state) to separate aliased state leaves in advance. The new function _graft_replaced(pairs) grafts the loaded tensors in place at the positions of the original state tree. If an aliased leaf is in two places, it becomes ambiguous which slot to put it in, so this case is blocked early with an assertion (multiple loaded tensors share one device array).

The two new arguments that load_checkpoint_streamed takes were also routed in this commit.

  • window_gb: the pinned-host budget for that batch. If None, auto-window is used.
  • on_replaced callback: receives a list of old/new device array pairs for the completed batch. The caller uses this list to graft onto the state tree.

window_cap_gb is a safety belt that is set from restore_concurrent_gb only when window_gb is not specified.

The core of this flow is not making a copy of the optimizer state in pinned-host, but moving tensors to the device one by one and then grafting the original reference. The benefit is especially large in the warm_start case (load pretrained params, start with fresh opt state). The existing do_not_load_opt_state=True path cuts the opt state fields in advance with warm_purge(self.state). The streamed path leaves host_state as None and grafts only the loaded params, so no pinned-host copy of the opt state is ever created. The checkpoint stack now atomically supports the standard flow in which the Gen4+6/+7 Muon and GB300 flagships start with pretrained params and a fresh optimizer.

2. The response compression path fixed a bug that dropped gRPC trailers, and added a zstd encode time histogram verified — phoenix/crates/serving/xai-recsys-engine/src/grpc_compression.rs (+109/−13), phoenix/crates/serving/xai-recsys-engine/src/emb_table.rs (+22/−5), phoenix/crates/serving/xai-recsys-engine/src/request_metrics.rs (+17/−4):

When GrpcCompressionService compressed a response body with zstd, it previously extracted only the body with collected.to_bytes() and rewrapped it in a new axum::body::Body::from(data). In this process, gRPC trailers (especially grpc-status and grpc-message) were all lost. A gRPC frame carries the status code in a trailer after the body, and that part was discarded. Clients may have received the response normally yet treated it as UNKNOWN/EOF because the status trailer was missing.

The new code first extracts the trailers with collected.trailers().cloned(). Then the rebuild_response(parts, data, trailers) helper rebuilds the response body by reattaching the trailers with Full::new(data).with_trailers(async move { Some(Ok(tr)) }). Both paths were unified so that trailers are kept whether compression succeeds or fails. Two regression tests (compressed_response_forwards_trailers, non_compressed_response_forwards_trailers) pin down this behavior.

A new histogram, recsys_engine_response_compress_ms{method}, was also added to the same file. It takes Instant::now() right before entering tokio::task::spawn_blocking(compress_grpc_frame) and observes with elapsed().as_secs_f64() * 1000.0 afterward. Measured this way, the queuing and CPU time of zstd encoding can be viewed separately per method. The buckets share the request latency buckets (crate::request_metrics::latency_buckets_ms()).

Why it matters: Trailer loss is a serious bug that silently breaks the serving contract. If a client cannot determine the response status, retry logic, error logging, and circuit breakers all misbehave. This commit also added regression tests, which greatly lowers the chance of the same bug recurring. The _compress_ms histogram shows how much zstd encoding of large responses on GB300 contributes to response latency, which gives a basis for tuning the compression level.

3. copy_port shuffles the shard schedule per pod to spread peer load evenly verified — phoenix/crates/serving/xai-recsys-engine/src/copy_port_client.rs (+113/−10):

shuffle_sharded_schedule(n, tensor_name) is new. Previously, when pods received multiple shards of one tensor in parallel, all of them requested shards in order starting from index 0. As a result, the owner peer of the first shard was momentarily overloaded.

The new logic mixes POD_NAME (or HOSTNAME) and the tensor name with a hash. It shuffles with StdRng::seed_from_u64(hash), seeded by this hash, so that each pod requests shards in a different order. Because the seed is deterministic, the same pod keeps the same order even after a restart (log reproducibility). The restore_piece_order(shuffled, schedule) -> Option<Vec<T>> helper restores results received in the shuffled order to the original order. Both consumers, emb_table.rs and copy_port_client.rs, were unified to use this new helper. The shuffle applies only to sharded ownership, and replicated keeps in-order. With replicated, all pods receive the same data, so shuffling gives no benefit.

The log records only the first 8 indexes (copy_port: shard schedule shuffled name={tensor} n={total} first={:?}). This log can diagnose whether the shuffle was actually applied. On encountering TRANSFER_FAILED_SENTINEL (we infer it is u32 max inferred), it returns early with an error before restore.

Why it matters: When many pods restore large embedding tables and dense weights, traffic spikes concentrate on the peer that owns shard 0. This problem was mitigated by Gen4+7's node-serialize and concurrent_gb, but the peer-side spike remained. The shuffle spreads that last bottleneck inversely proportional to the number of pods. Deterministic shuffle matters for two reasons:

  • The shuffle itself can be reproduced from logs.
  • Even if the same pod loads the same tensor several times, the order is the same, so cache hit rate observation stays stable.

Undisclosed:

  • The first active config of restore_streamed (currently presumed false by default inferred; only one added line in the config was confirmed)
  • A realistic consumer of keep_emb_opt_state=True in warm_start_staging
  • Evidence that the gRPC trailer loss bug was observed in production (customer tickets? retry storms?)
  • The P99 target of recsys_engine_response_compress_ms
  • How the request rate distribution of the shard 0 peer changed before and after the copy_port shuffle was introduced

Gen4+11 (2026-08-28, bc8e5f0) — visibility-filtering rule-layer refactor + 90-case golden corpus (no policy change)

The 24 VF rule files were thinned to use domain methods while leaving the verdict logic unchanged, and a new 90-case regression corpus now pins the verdicts verified. The policy did not change, and CI now breaks if a rule is added to the policy without adding a corpus case verified — the daily on this commit.

The 24 rule files in the VF sub-repo were thinned all at once (+1,522/−1,151 in total, a pure refactor). The RuleContext definition was split out of mod.rs into a new file, context.rs. The rule verdict logic stays as it was, and every direct access of the form context.candidate().foo was unified into domain methods (context.is_stale_tweet(), context.viewer_country_in(...)). To back this unification, the commit added a 90-case regression corpus (golden_corpus.rs, +1039 new) and a candidate builder. The candidate builder is fixtures.rs (+116 new). verified — visibility-filtering/rules/context.rs, visibility-filtering/rules/golden_corpus.rs, visibility-filtering/rules/fixtures.rs, visibility-filtering/rules/registry.rs.

RuleContext exposes about 25 domain methods. verified Grouped, they are:

  • Viewer state: viewer_is_logged_out, viewer_is_underage, viewer_has_no_stated_age, viewer_allows_sensitive_media, viewer_country_in
  • Viewer↔author relationship: is_author_viewer, viewer_follows_author, viewer_blocks_author, viewer_mutes_author, viewer_mutes_retweets_from_author
  • Tweet shape: is_retweet, is_stale_tweet, is_nullcast, is_community_tweet, has_media, has_dmca_media
  • NSFW: is_nsfw_flagged, has_tweet_nsfw_user_flag, has_tweet_nsfw_admin_flag
  • Country regulation: legal_takedown_in_viewer_country, local_laws_takedown_in_viewer_country, media_restricted_in_viewer_country
  • Author state: author_is_suspended/deactivated/erased/offboarded/protected/nsfw_user/nsfw_admin, author_has_user_label
  • Exclusive content: is_exclusive_tweet, viewer_is_conversation_author, viewer_super_follows_author

The WORLDWIDE_COUNTRY_CODE = "xx" constant and the takedown reason extraction function were also moved here from tes_rules.rs. verified

The 90-case corpus is divided into 13 categories. The categories are filter_all, baseline, author_state, relationship, tweet_label, tweet_shape, age_gating, exclusive_content, interstitial, oon_media, oon_tweet_label, oon_user_label, and interaction. Each case has the form Case { name, level, viewer, candidate, expected_action, expected_decided_by }, and three assertions apply. verified

  • golden_corpus_pins_policy_verdicts: checks that every case still produces the same action and the same decided_by.
  • every_wired_rule_decides_a_corpus_case: the set of rule names wired into Policies, minus the set of names the corpus actually uses as the decider, must be empty. CI breaks if a rule is added to the policy without adding a corpus case.
    • For this assertion, a new helper wired_rule_names(level) was added to registry.rs under #[cfg(test)].
  • corpus_case_names_are_unique: case names must not overlap.

Individual rule files keep their logic; only the expression got thinner. For example, in DropStaleTweetsRule in tes_rules.rs, the three earlier early returns (the retweet check, the source_tweet_id.is_some() check, and the is_stale check) shrank to two lines. verified — visibility-filtering/rules/tes_rules.rs

Places that took an fn(&TweetFeatures) -> bool callback, such as tweet_flag_rules.rs and user_rules.rs, changed their signature to fn(&RuleContext<'_>) -> bool. The callback bodies moved over as well, as in |t| t.nsfw.user → |context| context.has_tweet_nsfw_user_flag(). Of the −298 in registry.rs, we infer that half is individual rule tests moved into the corpus and the other half is repeated inline setup such as Viewer::LoggedIn(999) that was removed. inferred

Why it matters: The policy itself is unchanged. This commit reads as the next step in the flow in which, since the initial Gen4 rewrite, VF has been "removing safety nets (the Gen4+7 reference_compare harness, the Gen4+9 media fallback cache removal) while accumulating regression-defense assets internally". As RuleContext grows richer in domain language (for example legal_takedown_in_viewer_country), the grounds for a verdict read alongside the file name whenever a rule is added or changed. In addition, the mechanism that ties rule wiring to an assertion (every_wired_rule_decides_a_corpus_case) blocks "wiring without tests" at the CI level even as the rule library grows.

Undisclosed: It remains possible that the semantics of some rule file changed subtly during the refactor. This commit alone does not show whether the 90 golden corpus cases match earlier production verdicts exactly. Because the corpus was first introduced in this commit, comparison with the earlier version has to be done by hand. If the Gen4+7 reference_compare harness keeps running after this commit, it is in effect being verified against real traffic.

Gen4+11 (2026-08-28, bc8e5f0) — Phoenix serving: rerankerHeadTag parameter wiring + emb_table gRPC receive moved to the blocking pool

On the serving side of the same commit (bc8e5f0), the value that selects the reranker head started to be carried in Phoenix requests, but this commit contains no serving logic that uses it verified. The large copy performed when receiving the embedding table over gRPC was moved to the blocking pool so that it no longer holds runtime threads verified — the daily on this commit.

The change has two parts.

  • The parameter that selects the reranker head is connected end to end, from home-mixer through two proto locations to the Phoenix request path. This commit has no serving-side logic that consumes it.
  • In the emb_table gRPC receive callback, the non-temporal copy and the Adler-32 computation were split off into spawn_blocking. Tokio runtime threads are no longer held up by a large memcpy.

1. The RerankerHeadTag parameter is connected from home-mixer to the Phoenix request verified — home-mixer/params/param.rs, home-mixer/models/candidate.rs, home-mixer/scorers/phoenix_scorer.rs, home-mixer/util/phoenix_request.rs, phoenix/crates/serving/xai-recsys-proto/proto/recsys.proto, phoenix/python/common/xai-proto/proto/recsys.proto:

A pub reranker_head_tag: Option<u32> field was added to PostCandidate, and PhoenixScorer sends this parameter value along when it makes a request.

The reranker_head_tag returned in the scoring result is attached back to the candidate with candidate.reranker_head_tag = scored.reranker_head_tag (a round trip). phoenix_request.rs also fills scoring_sequence.reranker_head_tag with the parameter value and puts it in the request.

The proto field was added symmetrically to two messages.

The Rust proto and the Python proto were updated with the same field number. verified

Why it matters: inferred Because the default is 0 and this commit has no change to server-side consumption logic, this is a wiring step before head routing is turned on. The name head_tag, and its placement alongside UserActionSequence (the input to the feed scorer), read as "specify which reranker head to use for one sequence". The interpretation is a switch that picks one of several reranker heads inside the model for an A/B test during the experiment period. The pattern of training several ranker heads together and routing among them by tag at serving time is common at the mature stage of A/B testing.

2. emb_table.rs hands the copy of data received over gRPC into the destination buffer to the blocking pool verified — phoenix/crates/serving/xai-recsys-engine/src/emb_table.rs (+79/−12)

Previously, inside send_entries, the gRPC proto callback performed the non-temporal copy directly into the destination slice and updated the Adler-32. The new code splits the data into 4 MiB chunks and pushes them into a sync_channel(2). The copy is handled by a consumer run separately through tokio::task::spawn_blocking.

The callback only sends a chunk wrapped with bytes::Bytes::copy_from_slice into the channel. The non-temporal copy and the Adler-32 computation run on blocking pool threads. On the RDMA path as well, even the final Adler-32 summation was moved to spawn_blocking.

A new helper, JoinOnDrop<T>, was added as a safeguard. On the normal path, the result is collected with join().await. When dropped, it always terminates the blocking task with block_in_place and block_on(handle). verified The purpose is presumably to prevent file descriptor and handle leaks inferred.

Why it matters: inferred The gRPC callback runs on a Tokio runtime thread. So if the non-temporal copy and the Adler-32 computation hold a runtime thread for long, other tasks (request routing, admission decisions, health checks, and so on) are delayed. With this change, the gRPC receive thread only passes chunks along without a memcpy, and the blocking pool handles the CPU-bound copy. The 4 MiB chunk size and the sync_channel capacity of 2 regulate the receive rate through backpressure. This change is part of the same flow as the Gen4+9 emb_table core split (the load_tensor_into signature, pyo3-free) and the Gen4+10 copy_port shuffle. The serving infrastructure for large embedding tables is refining the boundary between the tokio runtime and CPU-bound work in several places.

Side change: In copy_port_client.rs (+16/−15), the join_all(...spawn) → collect → map_err idiom was extracted into a new join_transfers helper. Only duplication was removed, and behavior did not change. Two test names also changed. ..._despite_spawn was removed, and ..._between_spawned_batches became ..._between_batches. This is identified as a cleanup of wording added in yesterday's commit, which introduced the deterministic shuffle. verified

A Bytes callback type was added in proto_parser.rs (+11). A Bytes callback now sits beside the existing Str callback (FnMut(usize, &[u8])), so chunks can be passed by ownership transfer. The signature of the Bytes callback is FnMut(usize, Bytes). In this commit emb_table still uses the Str signature, so true zero-copy is a point to watch in a later commit. verified

Undisclosed:

  • How serving-side Phoenix actually consumes RerankerHeadTag (this commit has no consuming logic)
  • Whether UserActionSequence.rerankerHeadTag and ScoreInfo.rerankerHeadTag are symmetric between request and response (the request says which head to score with, the response says which head was actually used), or serve a different purpose
  • Why emb_table does not yet use the Bytes callback (preparation for other consumers vs. a plan to switch emb_table in the next commit)
  • How much the tail latency of the tokio runtime improved after the gRPC callback was moved to the blocking pool

Gen4+12 (2026-09-01, 6384ca7) — 16 NSFW-gating countries published + Rust↔Scala VF drift monitoring + motion-reveal-based special video safety pipeline

The 16 countries in which NSFW media is filtered for viewers who have not stated their age were stated explicitly as a default in VF code for the first time, and a mechanism was added to monitor whether the lists of the two VF stacks, Rust and Scala, diverge verified. A safety pipeline also appeared that accepts only high-popularity videos whose fav count is at or above a threshold, and shows Grok the original together with motion-reveal frames that expose content hidden under a static overlay, to reach a verdict verified — the daily on this commit.

This commit adds two axes to the safety stack. One is that the age-gating policy was stated in code for the first time, and the other is that a layer that actively counters evasion was newly connected.

The 16 NSFW-gating countries were stated in code as a default verified — visibility-filtering/params.rs (216 lines, new). default_nsfw_gating_countries() returns the following list.

In country names, these are Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, Germany, Spain, France, the United Kingdom, Indonesia, Italy, South Korea, Mexico, the Netherlands, the Philippines, Portugal, and Thailand. This list can be overridden at runtime through the feature switch rust_vf_nsfw_gating_countries. The value is wrapped in an ArcSwap and looked up again every 30 seconds.

It monitors whether the Rust VF and Scala VF lists diverge (drift). On every refresh, refresh_and_check_drift in the same file also reads the sibling YAML country_specific_nsfw_content_gating.yml (which the Scala VF stack references). If the Rust result and the Scala list diverge, it emits a tracing::warn! and increments the nsfw_gating_countries_drift counter of xai_stats_receiver. The two stacks are running in parallel, and the design makes drift observable.

If a malformed value is mixed in, the whole list reverts to the default (fail-whole fallback). If a malformed element (for example a number) is mixed into the feature switch value, it falls back to the full default 16 countries rather than using a partial list. The regression test malformed_value_falls_back_whole_not_partial locks in this contract.

A country list was injected into three rules verified — visibility-filtering/rules/nsfw_age_gating.rs. Three rules operate in parallel on media candidates labeled NSFW/GORE.

  • SensitiveViewerLoggedOutDropRule: drops unconditionally if the viewer is logged out. It is independent of country.
  • SensitiveViewerUnderageDropRule: drops if the viewer is confirmed to be under 18. It is independent of country.
  • SensitiveViewerNoStatedAgeDropRule: drops if a viewer whose age is unconfirmed belongs to the 16 countries above. That is, this rule does not apply in countries such as the United States, Japan, and Russia.

A new 8-stage DAG for high-popularity videos, PlanSafetyPtosSpecialVideo, was introduced verified — grox/flows/ptos/plan_safety_ptos_special_video.py (55 lines, new). The dependency graph is as follows.

special_video_filter → annotation_rate_limit → media_hydration → special_video_screen
    → category_detection → policy_detection
        → safemodel_sex_nudity
        → adult_content_cross_validation → result_sink

There are three entry conditions (_skip_reason).

  • There is a user.
  • The media contains at least one Video.
  • The fav count is at or above grox_config.media_hydration.deluxe_fav_count_threshold.

That is, only high-fan videos confirmed as viral enter. Because the whole process of screening, verdict, and LLM cross-validation is expensive per candidate, it is not widened to low-fan videos.

special_video_screen filters videos by whether motion-reveal frames exist verified — grox/flows/ptos/task_special_video_screen.py. _technique_signals returns a dict, and the only technique currently detected is motion_reveal. Only videos in which this field is non-empty move on to the next task.

The prompt sets the meaning of motion-reveal frames and the verdict criteria (rubric) verified — MOTION_REVEAL_DESCRIPTION in grox/core/lm/convo.py. A motion-reveal frame is a frame in which the static layer is subtracted from the original video and the faint motion layer is amplified. This processing exposes the real content that was hidden under a static overlay (a caption image, a transparent mask, a watermark, and so on). The Grok LLM receives both the original and the motion-reveal frame sets, and the prompt states two caveats explicitly.

  • Motion-reveal creates distortion. It can make "opaque clothing look like bare skin". Recall may be high but precision low, so it is not used to issue an unconditional hard verdict; it serves only as an entry signal that sends the video to downstream verdicts and cross-validation.
  • The original and motion-reveal frames must be treated separately in the verdict. The prompt states the rubric explicitly: "a person already visible in the original frames is judged on the original alone; only what newly appears in the motion-reveal frames is truly hidden content."

Image-processing functions that produce motion-reveal frames were added verified — grox/libs/video_tools/image.py (+125). They include CLAHE (contrast limited adaptive histogram equalization), adaptive brightness, saturation boost, and sharpen. X's safety pipeline put into production a preprocessing step that actively transforms video frames to expose evaded content.

Only the special video path operates fail-close verified — grox/flows/ptos/task_safety_ptos_adult_content_cross_validation.py:106-117, 130-148. If the Grok judge call fails with an exception, then for task_type == SAFETY_PTOS_SPECIAL_VIDEO the original verdict is not kept and is forcibly demoted to Soft (Grok 4.5 Cross Validation failed). On other paths, keeping the original verdict is the default. The Soft enforcement on the special video path sets the result to a single Soft level regardless of the original verdict. If the original verdict was Hard, this is a relaxation, and if there was no AdultContent violation, a Soft violation is newly attached verified — same file, lines 130-148.

This commit means four things at the policy level.

  • X stated in code, for the first time, the countries where it enforces age-gating. This list originally existed in Scala VF as well. This time it entered Rust VF as a default, and divergence between the two lists can now be observed through a metric. These two changes show a flow toward completing the Rust migration safely. The United States is not in the list.
  • The safety stack now has a layer that actively counters evasion. Before, it was a passive stack of "the model attaches a label → rules issue the verdict". Now a layer was added in front of it: "detect the evasion technique → actively remove the evasion → re-judge on those frames".
  • The evasion countermeasure is limited to high-fan videos.
    • It manages cost by applying the expensive countermeasure only to content confirmed to be spreading.
    • Because the evasion incentive is large given the scale of spread, it strengthens evasion detection.
    • That evasion detection does not trigger while a video is in a low-fan state is an open weakness of this architecture. Whether retroactive processing is connected could not be confirmed.
  • The _technique_signals dict has a shape that anticipates new techniques. Which technique (caption overlay, splash frame, chroma key, and so on) will be added after motion-reveal is a point to watch inferred.

Undisclosed:

  • The value of deluxe_fav_count_threshold
  • The exact algorithm for generating motion-reveal frames (the criteria for separating the "static layer" from the "faint motion layer")
  • Candidates for other evasion techniques and when they will be introduced
  • Whether retroactive processing for the low-fan state is connected

Gen4+13 (2026-09-01, 7ba7768) — visibility-filtering rules restructuring (struct-per-rule → data-driven RuleSpec, no policy change)

This is a refactor that changed how VF rules are written from one struct per rule to a list of data literals verified. The rule list and order are unchanged and this commit alone does not change safety verdicts, but in the same commit the default ads blender type in home-mixer was changed to multi_risk verified — the daily on this commit.

In the second commit of the same day (20:47 UTC), the rules/ subtree of VF was reorganized from 9 files into 3 files and a shared enum. It deleted 2,670 lines and added 1,568, but the rule list and order are unchanged, and a regression-prevention test locks this in as literals. It is the next step after the RuleContext cleanup and the introduction of the 90-case golden corpus in Gen4+11 (bc8e5f0).

The representation of rules changed from structs to data literals verified — visibility-filtering/rules/rule_spec.rs (89 lines, new).

  • The approach of writing struct + impl Rule for each rule is gone, and each rule became a one-line literal such as RuleSpec::Tweet { name, when, action, exempt_author }.
  • There are three variants.
    • Tweet: a tweet-condition predicate and drop/interstitial
    • Author: an author-condition predicate and drop
    • Custom: an arbitrary function pointer. It is used when the condition cannot be captured as a predicate.
  • Common exemptions were absorbed into spec fields. exempt_author is the self-view exemption of a tweet rule, and exempt_follower is the follower exemption of an author rule. The check that used to be repeated in each rule is gone.
  • There are only two kinds of action: Drop and SensitiveMediaInterstitial. An interstitial automatically checks viewer opt-in.

Tweet-axis rules were reorganized into per-group constants in tweet_rules.rs (1,125 lines) verified — visibility-filtering/rules/tweet_rules.rs. Rather than carrying over the old per-file rules as they were, the commit regrouped them by policy trigger type.

Two splits are especially meaningful.

  • nsfw_interstitial.rs was split into label-triggered interstitial and author-flag-triggered interstitial. The former goes into the home base rules, and the latter went out to a separate constant.
  • tes_rules.rs was split into shared by home (stale and takedown) and recs only (DMCA and geo-restricted media). That is, a recommendations-only rule axis became explicit in the code.

SensitiveViewerNoStatedAgeDropRule kept its name and condition but changed how it stores state verified. The rule that in Gen4+12 (6384ca7) was a struct with an Arc<NsfwGatingCountries> field in nsfw_age_gating.rs was moved into a Custom spec.

  • Previously, the rule itself held Arc<NsfwGatingCountries> as a field. Now RuleContext holds the reference, and the rule looks up through context.nsfw_gating_country(code). The rule became a stateless, zero-sized data literal.
  • The three rule names (SensitiveViewerLoggedOutDropRule, SensitiveViewerUnderageDropRule, SensitiveViewerNoStatedAgeDropRule) are kept as they were, because audits, metrics, and regression tests refer to these names as literals.

Author-axis rules were gathered by group in author_rules.rs (354 lines) verified — visibility-filtering/rules/author_rules.rs.

SOCIALGRAPH_DROPS stayed as Custom because it has to look at viewer state (logged-out, blocks, mutes) together with the relationship.

The registry.rs regression-prevention test locks in "no policy change" as literals verified — visibility-filtering/rules/registry.rs.

The new test wired_rule_order_matches_pre_migration_sequence verifies, as literals and including order, the rule names of 28 rules for TimelineHome, 26 additional rules for TimelineHomeRecommendations, and 1 rule for FilterAll. The rule order of the home timeline is as follows (for reference).

Why it matters

  • The policy is unchanged. This commit alone does not change safety verdicts. Paired with the 90-case golden corpus of Gen4+11 and the every_wired_rule_decides_a_corpus_case assertion, it is the next step in the direction of "locking wiring, tests, and order with CI even as the rule library grows".
